projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Julian M. Hamed was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: This is Nathan Rittenhouse recording Tony Hamed on his World War Two experience. So, urn, where you drafted or did you volunteer for the army?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Urn, when the war broke out I was uh very uh concerned, I wanted, I felt like I wanted to help the country. My parents wanted me to take an agricultural draft uh deferment and stay home. But I uh decided to try to volunteer for the Air force and I was turned down for a minor physical disability, which I later had corrected. But, I went along for a couple years then and I was drafted in March 1943 and uh I was uh much to my families dismay, but uh I was sent to Texas. Joined the 6th 56th tank destroyer battalion. I took basic training there at camp Bowie and latter on at camp Hood Texas which is now one of the big places in Texas.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, where you living the county at the time you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Oh yes.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Okay

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: I have, have lived, in other words I was born in Arbrovale and uh then moved to Green Bank, all my life, well, except for a year or two in Ohio, most of my life's been here.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, how long were you in training before they sent you off?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, while I was, right after I finished basic training uh then the Air Force uh lowered their uh qualification and a notice came down to my unit that I was in, that, you could volunteer for the Air Force. So I volunteered for the Air Force and was sent to Hastings Nebraska to college for four months and from there I went to San Anna California to preflight center. And I was in what they call pre-preflight and that was just prior to the Normandy the landing in Normandy in 1944. And they decided they had had more people, 00 casualties in the Air Force were less than they estimated to begin with. Ground casualties were more and the people that volunteered for the Air Force were usually more apt to become platoon leaders or noncom or junior officers, ground forces. So uh I have a copy of the order, one day I was in this plush army Air Force base in San Anna California the next day I was up in the mountains of Northern California with the 89th flight infantry division, a pack division.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, they swapped you all over the place.

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yea, well they took the privates that had trained in this division and shipped them out over seas as replacements and we filled the division up, the people coming back from the Air Force. And they retained the 00 noncoms who'd been in the division, sent us back to Camp Butner North Carolina and 00 reorganized as a regular infantry division and we trained there and 00 this was a pretty interesting period and a lot ofthese noncoms resented the Air Force people as things got kind of rough at times, so, 00, they came out with a notice that anybody interested could go to a officer candidate school infantry at fort Benning Georgia. So I applied and was accepted for that. Went to Benning in full of'44 and 00 went to officer candidate school and graduated in February of'45. I was a second lieutenant in the infantry and 00 got orders for a ten-day leave at home and over seas, as a replacement.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, where did you wind up over seas?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: I landed at Le Harve went up through the replacement system, the replacement depots and joined the 9th armor division which was then in the process of capturing the Remagin Bridge- the first bridge across the Rhine river, first crossing the Rhine. The 9th Armor division had been uh severely beat up in the Battle ofthe Bulge. They were up on the line there, the German boarder, and jumped off in uh an attack in the morning they were right in the face of this panzer attack and uh a lot of them were lost.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, when you got there what were some of your daily activities? What was kind of the routine you had there?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, when I got there I was initially assigned to a machine gun battalion and this was the armor division, but I was in the 27th honored infantry battalion. The Armor division at that point was made ofthree combat commands each combat command had a tank battalion, an armored infantry battalion, and an armored artillery battalion. So I was in the armored infantry battalion.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Urn were you hurt in any way?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: At all when you were ...

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: No never, never injured. Didn't see much action, actually because see after we crossed the bridge then it was a kind of a race across Germany. You know we ran into some hot spots but uh we ended up on the Elbe River and were told to stop there and let the Russians come meet us. We could have been in Berlin if they'd let us go, but you know that was part of the Potsdam conference between Stalin and Roosevelt and Churchill-that we let the Russians take Berlin. So, we sat there and waited until they came.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, out of all that probably what was your most urn memorable experience?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, I think one of the most memorable experiences was like I say we were, you know we were traveling pretty rapidly and we didn't stop unless we really got some resistance. Well, uh I had this in machine gun platoon- my command vehicle was a half-track, you know what a half-track is?

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: I'm not exactly sure what that is.

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Its, its got wheels in front and tracks in the rear like a like a truck but it's armored, it got armor all around. But this one had a track that went around the top of it and a 50. Caliber machine gun rode on a carriage around there. Any time we were on the move we had one man assigned to that machine gun as an air guard uh and if we got an air attack why it was his duty to get that gun going and try to shoot the air plane down. Well I rode in the right front seat mostly standing up all the time. The standing operating procedure was that I was uh it was my responsibility to get out of his way if the gun come around that way. Well we got strafed and I just a this fighter was coming right down the road at us you know, the tracers were hitting the road and bouncing up. And I, I just sort of got transfixed, you know, and he come around with the gun and did what he was supposed to do, but when he fired it - if you ever heard one of those 50. Caliber-it was right by my ear it ruptured my eardrum. He never had to tell me to sit down after that. uh That was, that was about the closest I ever come to getting, uh getting hurt, uh I could see that them bullets coming knew ifhe'd come close enough that thing was going to be bouncing off the pavement right in front of us and then it'd be right on us.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So what were some of the emotional high and low points of the war while you were here? [Were] there ever a time where you were kind of pessimistic about it?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: well I think to me during the war the the most emotional- might call it high was Pearl Harbor. I, I can remember listing to the radio Sunday, Pearl Harbor Day. We lived down in the house where uh Woodell, Rick that was our home place. Dh and uh the low was the day that I got the order to take me out of the Air Force bought me back to, to the infantry.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, you didn't really see a lot of combat but...

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Were there any like graphic experiences you came upon?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Dh, well in the process of moving from Remagen Bridge to the Elbe uh we released the Balkan law Prison. POW prison, not the POW prison the uh what do you call them-the Jews uh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Concentration Camps?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Concentration Camps yea, uh that was quit an experience, lot of people say they don't believe in the concentration camps, but uh you ever been there you could remember the smell, you could remember the sights, and I know they were true.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, that was pretty nasty? As bad as all the movies are?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well close may be worst.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Did you lose any friends in the war?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yeah, I lost one good, very friend who was buried in he Military cemetery in Epinal France- U.S. cemetery in Epinal France. uh He was not in my unit. He was drafted too - bout the same time I was maybe a little earlier. But he was uh in the 36th division I believe that landed on the southern coast of France you know they had the landing in Normandy on the Northern coast of France then later a landing on the southern coast by the 7th Army. He was in the 36th division he was killed there. He was a uh local boy. uh At one time, he he had a service station where the post office now - located.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: The Green Bank Post Office down here?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yeah and a we - I spent a lot oftime with him. He was distantly related to me any way but uh you know I never knew what happened to him or anything but a if! ever had to go back I would, I would've like to have gone back - visited the beaches at Normandy. Which of course I wasn't there but I would, I read a lot about, I'd like to see that, I'd like to go to this cemetery in Epinal where he's buried.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, during the whole war what was the general morale of the soldiers? Were they optimistic about the outcome?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yes, there was uh no doubt, in our mind, that we're going to win the war. We had to. There was no alternative. You'd be living in a different world today ifwe hadn't.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, how long were you actually there?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, I was there till after the war ended. The war ended in Europe on the 8th of May and uh right after it ended we were on the Elbe. There they sent us down. It wasn't far to uh the city of Bayreuth where the big opera house is. Was the division headquarters. And uh we were on the - sent in to Czech ... into Czechoslovakia right on the Czech border and the Germans were coming back toward us because they wanted to surrender to the Americans they didn't want. .. , the Russians were crowding them the other way, see. They didn't want to be have to surrender to the Russians so uh we were accepting their surrenders. Then there were a lot of civilians trying to escape you know from the Russians. We had a post on the road there, we were suppose to stop these civilians and accept the surrender of any Russians or uh Germans. Ha, one of the things that happened there was one day there was a lady start having a baby at our post. So called back to the battalion - ask them "what do I do now?" And so they had us put her in a half-track and take her back to the battalion, and the battalion surgeon delivered the baby.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, after you were done there where did you go?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well at that point the war was over and they set up what they call a point system the soldiers been over there a long time they got so many points for each month they been there. High point guys were eligible to go home, but low point guys like me were stuck. I'd been there for about a year. Uh There's only one way you could - one alternative of that - they had divisions and uh states at that point who'd all ready gone home - were reorganizing, refitting and getting ready to go to the Pacific to take part in the landing on the southern coast of Japan in November December. So they came out said you can go to states get a 30-day leave and join the Sth division which had been in Europe but had been sent home, reorganized, refitted and filled up with replacements. So, I took it. And I left over there in July of'44 not long, not long after the war was over. I got home, got my 30-day leave, and the Sth division was in Fort Bernard Wood, Missouri, and their equipment was loaded in San Francisco. They were scheduled to sail in October, and rendezvous at sea with the invasion force from the Philippines, land on the southern coast of Japan. While on the train back to Fort Leonard, to go up to Fort Leonard Wood heard that we'd dropped the bomb on Japan. I arrived at Fort Leonard Wood, heard they dropped the second bomb, then Japan surrendered after about two weeks. They cancelled our orders and I was home free.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Well you shuflled around to all kinds of divisions and so forth.

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yeah, uh I decided to stay in awhile. And uh they broke up the 8th division then uh sent me back. I got, I got sent back to Fort Camel to the 5th division which is another old division back, was there awhile they came out then with the what they call the UMT. The United or a Military Training Program what they did was they was taking a lot ofthese they decided you know they's going to have a post line standing army. And they taking in a lot of these kids that grew up on the streets during World War Two and training them. So I went to a training at Fort Knox went to a training center there and helped train those kids, which was quite an experience - uh never forget that. I run a rifle range there for - and had this one kid, a first iron-clad rule was you always deep your rifle pointed down range and I had to stand right back ofthe firing line, you know where I gave commands to fire - and he right in front of me - and he jumped up and turned around with his rifle. You know he had a ajam or something, you know, and uh finally I lost my temper one day. I jumped off of there, kicked him in the behind and told him to never stand up again with that. Turned around looked there was a colonel standing back there. Went in uh I told the company commander - I said well we're probably in trouble told him what happened. Next morning he told me get in full dress had to report to general. Went up to the general and got atcfmmodation for running the rifle range. Julian Rittenhouse: Probably as dangerous as the war.

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yeah, it was. Well stayed there 'till our oldest son was born there - David at Fort Knox till a May about May of '47. I think decided to get out, they come out with uh the Gi-bill yea I decided to go to college. I got out and come home and when I got out I joined the reserves went out to Tulsa, Oklahoma went to college and uh in fall of '50 the Korean War broke out, yea the summer of'50 the Korean War broke out. I got recalled. But I had been temporarily assigned to a field artillery battalion although I wasn't active didn't get paid for training or anything. I didn't have time I was going to school had a and working part time and a didn't have time to take part in a reserve program but when they recalled me because I'd been attached to this artillery battalion they sent me to Fort Sills artillery school. Went out there and they put me through a what they call communication officer school artillery and finished that in March of March of '51 - yep. And they fill us out - there was 53 of us. Two of us got orders to Germany. The rest of them - they put them on an air plane and flew them in to Korea. Me and one other guy orders to Germany. Why? I don't know. Never knew, never asked. But went to Germany and that was at the height of the Cold War and uh we were kinda playing footsie with the Russians up on the a eastern border and that's what, that's what we did there for about two years. I joined a 517th armored field artillery battalion which was stationed in a little Kaferne. They called it a little military post the Germans had had about 40 miles out of Frankford and a we kept a one battery up on the the a border. Julian Rittenhouse: Would that have been the better of the two choices? I mean the Korean went into combat.. ..

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: 0 yea, I mean it wasn't, it wasn't all peaches and cream but it was a lot better that Korea. I mean ... Julian Rittenhouse: Some officer somewhere probably took a liken to you or saw the potential you had or something. I mean there had to be - an interesting thing - that slim a picking - that two of you ... that's interesting isn't it?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Yea, I don't know I never questioned it. You know the kind of the story of my army career you know I think sometimes I think the good Lord was looking out for me. When I left that infantry division at Camp Butner - went to OCS that division went overseas, although I didn't know at the time they were going overseas, but that's the way things happen. Julian Rittenhouse: Now Nathan asked you about your family. Did they warm up to things afterwards? Then they accepted it, or that was a struggle for your mom and dad probably?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: They accepted it you know, but they you know uh my dad was a - he wasn't to keen about it. Julian Rittenhouse: Now, did you stay in the reserve after you got out?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: No, anyway stayed in there till, till when it came out first time and joined the reserves 1 signed up for a 5 year term. Well, that term was over the fall of'52 -see was' 47 to ' 52. Headed over there and I, I'd forgotten all about it. 1 didn't - you know ().d.' u. -\o.n-r realize it. 1 didn't even notice - was situation - existed. But an a~ came out one day "1 got to see you" 1 said "what about?" At that time Jane and a David had gone over there after been over there a year they got over there- had the quarters there uh he says your reserve commission is fine ... got to get you signed for another term. I says, so what if I don't sign? He said, I'll have to start cutting orders to send you home. 1 said you better start cutting orders. As a result, Steve was born in November and we left there - I think January some where. Anyway, we got home uh, got to leave and then went back to Fort Meade and got a discharge. They asked me ifI wanted to join the reserves, I said absolutely not.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: So, where in all your traveling around did you meet your wife?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: At the head of the hollow. We were married in '44 before I went overseas.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Overall, in generaL how did your involvement in the war affect your life as a civilian?

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, it affected me many ways. I mean, you know, I feel like I'm much broader person I learned a lot of things - course I went to school. I had two~ears of college. And I uh I wouldn't take a million dollars for the experience, and I wouldn't go through it again for a million dollars or any amount of money. I saw uh part ofthe world, met a lot of good people, some bad people, all kinds of experiences.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: Well, I thank you for your time and for your story.

sp.speaker: Julian M. Hamed
sp.p: Well, you're quite welcome.

sp.speaker: Nathan Rittenhouse
sp.p: I guess that'll conclude it then.
